n: This royal psalm borrows heavily from Psalm 18. David praises the Lord, his ‘Rock,’ who trains him for battle — his skill as a warrior came from God.

f.w: which teacheth my hands to war

n: A stack of titles for God: his steadfast love, fortress, high tower, deliverer, and shield. God keeps the people peaceful under David’s rule.
Amazement: what are humans, that God notices or cares about them? Compare Psalm 8 and Moses’ vision.
People are like a breath, and their days like a passing shadow. Yet God cares for them.
David asks God to part the sky and come down, touching mountains so they smoke — like at Sinai.

f.w: Bow thy heavens, O LORD, and come down

n: ‘Flash your lightning and scatter the enemy; shoot your arrows and rout them.’
Reach down from on high and pull me out of the deep waters — out of the hands of foreigners.
These enemies speak lies, and even their ‘right hand,’ raised to swear oaths, is false.

f.g: Their sworn oaths (sworn with raised right hand) are lies.

n: He promises a new song of praise on a ten-stringed harp.
God gives victory to kings and rescued David from the deadly sword.
The plea from verses 7–8 is repeated like a refrain.
The psalm turns to a vision of peace: sons growing strong like healthy young plants, daughters like beautifully carved corner pillars of a palace.

f.w: as plants grown up in their youth

f.g: Carved corner pillars, graceful and strong.

n: Barns full of every kind of produce, and flocks multiplying by thousands in the fields.
Strong oxen, no breaches in the city walls, no exile, and no cries of distress in the streets — complete security.

f.w: no breaking in, nor going out
f.g: No breach of the walls, no going into captivity.

n: Happy is the people with such blessings — and above all, happy is the people whose God is the Lord.

f.w: happy is that people, whose God is the LORD
